clue.text: Presage a word of warning to R.A.F. type going East ?

parts.note: golfers shout 'fore' to warn players ahead of a ball in flight
'bod' was RAF slang for a person, a type or fellow
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: An airman heading east issues an ominous warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going' only links the airman to his direction: E is simply added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To presage and to forebode both mean to foretell or warn of something, usually bad, before it happens.

clue.text: Flourished over a relative, to show off

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the second

parts.note: fl. is the abbreviation for floruit, 'flourished', used of a person's active years
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Someone waved a hand above a family member to make a display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flourished' looks like a verb of waving; it gives FL, the reference-book abbreviation for floruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To flaunt is to display ostentatiously, parading something so others notice.

clue.text: Avis's special quality ?

parts.note: avis is Latin for bird, and the 'rara avis', the rare bird, is prized for being uncommon

explanation.surface: A woman called Avis has a quality all her own.
explanation.walkthrough: Avis looks like a woman's name; it is the Latin for bird, from the phrase 'rara avis', a rare bird, someone or something unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare bird of the Latin tag is valued for its scarcity, its unusualness.

clue.text: Beside the lake, the trees " (Wordsworth)

parts.note: a line from Wordsworth's 'Daffodils', where the poet finds the flowers by the water; the missing word fills the gap

explanation.surface: A line of verse placing flowers by a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a dash between 'lake,' and 'the trees': the poem runs 'Beside the lake, beneath the trees'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted verse takes a preposition meaning under, which the poet supplies.

clue.text: Deceiver the tennis-player tries not to be !

definitions.text: Deceiver the tennis-player tries not to be !

parts.words: Deceiver the tennis-player tries not to be
parts.note: a server who misses twice in a row commits a double fault, so a tennis player avoids dealing doubles; a two-faced cheat has the same name

explanation.surface: A tennis player strives to stay honest.
explanation.walkthrough: A double-dealer is a two-faced cheat, but read literally it is one who deals doubles, and a server dreads the double fault.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-dealer is a duplicitous person who says one thing and does another.

clue.text: Stormy scene in the drawing-room ?

parts.note: plays on the saying 'a storm in a ...', a great fuss over a trifle, here set among the china of a genteel parlour

explanation.surface: A domestic row breaks out in a genteel parlour.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'a storm in a teacup' means a lot of fuss about nothing; the drawing-room is where the tea things would be.
explanation.definitionFit: A small china vessel for drinking tea is where the proverbial little storm of fuss takes place.

clue.text: Always ahead of fashion here

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece comes ahead of, above, the second

parts.note: ever means always
ton is fashion, from French bon ton

explanation.surface: This place has always led the way in style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' is the definition: a place, a district of Liverpool and home of the football club.
explanation.definitionFit: The Liverpool district and its football club are a place, which 'here' stands for.

clue.text: Punishes those with money

explanation.surface: Someone penalises the wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: To cashier an officer is to dismiss him in disgrace; cashiers are also the people who handle a firm's cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashiering is dismissal from the armed forces as a punishment; bank tellers are those who take and pay out cash.

clue.text: Reading makes a country wax lyrical

parts.note: Peru is a country in South America
to wax lyrical is to break into song, so sing

explanation.surface: Studying causes a nation to grow poetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' could be the English town; here it is the verb, studying a text.
explanation.definitionFit: Perusing is examining a text carefully, so studying or looking through it.

clue.text: Originally one carried away by his own hot air

definitions.text: Originally one carried away by his own hot air

parts.words: Originally one carried away by his own hot air
parts.note: a windbag carried away by his own talk, but literally an early balloonist lifted by a hot-air balloon

explanation.surface: A pompous talker gets carried away by his own bluster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot air' looks like empty talk; the first balloon flights were made with hot air, so 'originally' points to the earliest balloonists.
explanation.definitionFit: The word first named balloonists, who rose literally carried by heated air in their envelopes.

clue.text: Nap may well be got by such a joker

definitions.text: Nap may well be got by such a joker

parts.words: Nap may well be got by such a joker
parts.note: the nap of cloth is raised by teasing it, and a joker who teases is the same word; Nap is also a card game, adding a false trail

explanation.surface: A prankster at the card table might well win at Nap.
explanation.walkthrough: Nap looks like the card game and the joker a playing card, but the nap is the raised fibre on cloth, brought up by a teasing tool, and a teasing joker shares the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tease is a joker who mocks playfully, and a teasel or carding device raises the nap on woollen cloth.

clue.text: Madame de Maintenon in scholastic incarnation?

definitions.text: Madame de Maintenon in scholastic incarnation?

parts.words: Madame de Maintenon in scholastic incarnation
parts.note: Louis XIV's mistress, later his wife, founded and led a girls' school at Saint-Cyr, so she was both a royal mistress and a school's head

explanation.surface: A French royal favourite reborn as a schoolteacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame de Maintenon was the mistress and secret wife of Louis XIV and founded the girls' school at Saint-Cyr; split as HEAD MISTRESS she is a chief royal favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman in charge of a school is its principal teacher, and Maintenon both ran Saint-Cyr and was the king's chief favourite.

clue.text: All bent on the game

annotationWithheld.why: All bent on the game (3-4): NETBALL is an anagram of ALL + BENT, so 'bent' is both the anagram indicator and part of the fodder; no other word signals the anagram

clue.text: Necessitates points loss by three mice

parts.note: E and N are compass points, east and north
in the nursery rhyme the three blind mice had their tails cut off by the farmer's wife

explanation.surface: A scoring penalty is imposed because of three rodents.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Three Blind Mice' has the farmer's wife cut off their tails with a carving knife, so their loss is their tails.
explanation.definitionFit: To entail is to involve as a necessary consequence, so it requires or necessitates.

clue.text: Alpine Rose's family

parts.note: the alpine rose is a mountain shrub of a large flowering genus whose Greek name means rose tree

explanation.surface: A woman named Rose has relatives in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose looks like a woman's name; the alpine rose is a species of this shrub genus, and the Greek name means 'rose tree'.
explanation.definitionFit: The alpine rose belongs to this genus of evergreen flowering shrubs, its family in the loose sense.

clue.text: But the detergent boys can't make a Dalmatian this white!

definitions.text: But the detergent boys can't make a Dalmatian this white!

parts.words: But the detergent boys can't make a Dalmatian this white
parts.note: soap-powder adverts promise a wash without stain, but a Dalmatian's spots are part of its coat and never come out

explanation.surface: Laundry advertisers cannot bleach a spotted dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Detergent adverts promise to leave clothes free of marks; the Dalmatian is a white dog with black spots, which no washing removes.
explanation.definitionFit: A spotless thing is perfectly clean, without a single mark, which a Dalmatian's coat can never be.

clue.text: Gentlemen in velvet make hay and are set upon

parts.note: Jacobites toasted 'the little gentleman in black velvet', the mole whose hill threw William III's horse; moles have velvety fur
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry as hay

explanation.surface: Smartly dressed men harvest the fields and are attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jacobite toast to 'the little gentleman in black velvet' honoured the mole whose molehill tripped William III's horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To be molested is to be attacked or harassed, set upon by someone.

clue.text: Pa's role in art disturbed them in the bottom class

indicators.note: things disturbed are thrown into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Father's part in the arts upsets the working class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' rearranges PA'S ROLE IN ART, twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The proletariat is the lowest social class of wage-earners, and its members are its people.

clue.text: "Eyes, look your last! Arms take your last —.!"(R&)

definitions.text: Eyes, look your last! Arms take your last —.!"(R&)

parts.words: Eyes, look your last! Arms take your last
parts.note: Romeo's farewell over Juliet in the tomb; the missing word is the last thing his arms give her

explanation.surface: Lines from Romeo's dying farewell to Juliet.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a dash before the closing quotation mark: Romeo says 'Arms, take your last embrace!' (R & J is Romeo and Juliet).
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted line takes a noun for holding someone in the arms, which Shakespeare supplies.

clue.text: Throw out of court a style that might pass in King's Road?

definitions.text: a style that might pass in King's Road?

explanation.surface: A judge dismisses a case over casual dress in a fashionable street.
explanation.walkthrough: To nonsuit is to dismiss a lawsuit; split, a non-suit is informal dress, the kind worn in the King's Road, a fashionable shopping street in Chelsea, London.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsuiting stops a plaintiff's case in law; a non-suit outfit is casual wear, something other than a formal two-piece.

clue.text: Chinese mile close to being one such dimension

parts.note: the li is a Chinese unit of distance, about half a kilometre
near means close to

explanation.surface: A Chinese unit of distance approaches being one dimension.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such' points back to the mile: a length is a single dimension.
explanation.definitionFit: Something linear has only length, so it extends in one dimension, as a mile does.

clue.text: Feverishly exciting

parts.note: a plain description: frantic and full of excitement, with an echo of the old medical sense of a recurring fever

explanation.surface: Something is thrilling to the point of fever.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectic flush was once a fever symptom, and the word now means frantically busy and agitated.

clue.text: "Would start and under her feet And blossom in purple and red" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: Would start and under her feet And blossom in purple and red" (Tennyson)

parts.words: Would start and under her feet And blossom in purple and red
parts.note: a line from Tennyson's 'Maud', where the flowers and earth quiver as the beloved passes; the missing word fills the gap

explanation.surface: A line of verse about flowers stirring beneath a woman's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a dash after 'start and' where the missing word belongs: in 'Maud' the dust 'would start and tremble under her feet'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted verse takes a verb for quivering or shaking, which the poet supplies.

clue.text: Madly intent about love with an annuity

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go about, or round, the letter for love
acting madly is acting wildly, so the letters of intent are thrown into a new order

parts.note: O is love, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: Someone is crazily determined to secure a pension for love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madly' rearranges INTENT, and 'about' wraps those letters round O.
explanation.definitionFit: A tontine is a scheme in which subscribers share a fund as yearly payments, the survivors' shares growing as others die.

clue.text: Effortless scoring

parts.note: in cricket, runs from byes, wides and no-balls go to the batting side without being hit off the bat

explanation.surface: A player racks up points with no apparent effort.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, runs not scored off the bat (byes, leg-byes, wides, no-balls) are added to the total without any effort from the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: These are runs credited to the batting side that no batsman earned, an unearned bonus to the score.

clue.text: Overcoat, from a sheep you indicated phonetically !

parts.note: a teg is a sheep in its second year

indicators.note: phonetically asks for the words to be written as they sound, not as normally spelt

parts.note: the words 'you meant' say the same as the letters U and MENT

explanation.surface: A warm coat, made from sheep's wool, as you said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'phonetically' turns 'you meant' (you indicated) into the sounds U + MENT, after TEG.
explanation.definitionFit: A tegument is a natural covering or outer skin, a coat over the body.

clue.text: A Sussex College

parts.note: a Cambridge college whose full name joins a family name to Sussex, after its foundress the Countess of Sussex

explanation.surface: A college in the county of Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Sussex looks like the county in southern England; the college is in Cambridge, named after Lady Frances Sidney, Countess of Sussex, and the clue gives its full name less the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: The first word of the Cambridge college's full name precedes Sussex in its title.

clue.text: To Ceres I unfold the mysterious

indicators.note: to unfold is to open out and lay bare, so these letters are laid out anew

explanation.surface: The poet reveals hidden secrets to the goddess of the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfold' rearranges TO CERES I. Ceres is the Roman goddess of grain.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is obscure and hidden, known only to a small initiated circle.
